newsitem.title: UK: Major makes late appeal to voters on British unity.
newsitem.headline: Major makes late appeal to voters on British unity.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major tried on Tuesday to rescue his Conservatives from an election drubbing by warning of a threat to Britain's unity, sovereignty and prosperity if the opposition Labour Party win the election.
In his last big rally of the campaign, Major said polling day on Thursday would be "a day of destiny" for the British people.

He said it would decide whether Britain's current economic success, based on a low-tax, lightly regulated economy, would continue and whether the country would escape the twin dangers of fragmentation into its constituent nations and of the centralising clutches of the European Union.

"This election is about the unity of the United Kingdom. It is, literally, a battle for Britain...If we lose, Britain will change, yes -- change forever, change for the worse," Major told some 2,000 Conservatives at the rally in Docklands, east London.
"I'm going to fight right up to the last minute to keep our economy booming, to stand firm in Europe and to keep our United Kingdom one."

Major's plea for Britons to unite around his vision of a proud nation state came as opinion polls continued to suggest that Labour's Tony Blair will come to power after Thursday's poll with a massive overall parliamentary majority.

The Conservatives, in power since 1979, could face a bloodletting if they lose the election, with right-wing anti-European and centrist pro-Brussels factions fighting for the soul of the party whose divisions Major has striven to heal.

But Major concentrated his attention on Labour plans for a more conciliatory approach to Brussels, for separate parliaments for Scotland and Wales, and for economic changes such as a national minimum wage and more rights for trade unions.
He said trade union leaders, European federalists and Scottish and Welsh separatists were all praying for a Labour victory.
"Are those the people you want to see smiling after May 2?...Don't do it, for Britain's sake I appeal to you," Major said.
"We have no desire to launch ourselves now, or ever, across uncharted waters to an unknown destiny -- the pilgrim fathers of some new United States of Europe," he added.
Major said a Conservative victory would mean further steps along the road to a prosperous Britain which his party had already done much to build over the 18 years it has held power.
"The British people -- all the British people -- can go on to reap the richest harvest we've ever known," he said.

Major earlier spent the bulk of the penultimate day of campaigning in furious attacks against Labour for their claims that another Conservative government would scrap the state retirement pension and put value added tax on food.

He said the Labour pension scare was a distortion of a recently announced government plan to help people acquire a bigger pension by investing some of their state insurance contributions in private insurance schemes.
It was "a contemptible smear of the sort I have rarely ever encountered before in politics," Major said at a breakfast for party supporters in a London hotel.
As for the food tax claim, it was equally without foundation and "another illustration of the sort of tactics which have been used against the government in this campaign".
Later Major told a group of elderly Conservatives in Brighton, southern England: "I believe these truly unscrupulous untruths will rebound on them (Labour) at this general election."
